moduleTitle: SQE1 · Legal System and Legal Services
title: The SRA Principles
subtitle: The seven fundamental obligations, and how a conflict between them is resolved
objectives: State all seven SRA Principles in the order the SRA publishes them
Explain why the Principles are not of equal weight, and which take precedence when two pull in different directions
Apply the hierarchy to a fact pattern where a client's wishes conflict with the rule of law or public trust in the profession

leadingAuthorities.citation: SRA Principles, SRA Standards and Regulations 2019
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the seven fundamental ethical obligations that apply to every solicitor, firm and person the SRA regulates

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Almost every student can list some of the Principles. Very few can say, under exam pressure, which one wins when two of them point in opposite directions — and that's precisely what SQE1 tests.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the seven Principles cold. The test pool here is weighted towards conflict scenarios — expect fact patterns where a client wants something the profession-facing Principles won't allow.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and get the seven Principles fixed in order before moving on — the hierarchy in Part 2 only makes sense once you can name all seven without hesitating.

overview.hook: A client tells their solicitor exactly what they want: destroy the document, don't mention it, make the problem go away. Acting in that client's best interests is Principle 7 — one of the seven things every solicitor swears to uphold. And yet the solicitor who does what the client asks here has committed serious misconduct. This lesson is about the six words that explain why: the Principles are not all equal.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026 under the SRA Standards and Regulations 2019, in force since 25 November 2019. The seven Principles have not been amended since introduction; no change is currently proposed.

parts.heading: The seven Principles, in order
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students will return to
body: The SRA Principles sit at the top of the SRA Standards and Regulations 2019. They are short, deliberately broad, and apply to everyone the SRA regulates — solicitors, firms, and every person working in a regulated firm, not solely those with a practising certificate.

There are seven. Learn them in the SRA's own numbering, because SQE1 questions frequently ask you to identify 'which Principle' is engaged by a fact pattern, and the numbering itself sometimes matters to the answer.

Notice the shape of the list: the first two Principles look outward, to the justice system and to public confidence. The next three are personal qualities of the solicitor. The sixth looks outward again, to equality and inclusion. Only the seventh is about the individual client. That ordering is not decorative — it previews the hierarchy in Part 2.

components.label: The seven SRA Principles
points: 1 — Act in a way that upholds the constitutional principle of the rule of law, and the proper administration of justice
2 — Act in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the solicitors' profession and in legal services provided by authorised persons
6 — Act in a way that encourages equality, diversity and inclusion
7 — Act in the best interests of each client

interaction.prompt: Which numbered Principle requires a solicitor to act with independence?
options: Principle 2
Principle 3
Principle 5
Principle 7
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — independence is Principle 3, sitting between the two outward-facing Principles and the two Principles about personal honesty and integrity.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Independence is Principle 3. It's worth fixing the numbering precisely, because SQE1 questions often name a Principle by number rather than by description.

parts.heading: Why the Principles aren't equally weighted
parts.voice: argumentative — states the rule, then explains the logic behind it
body: It would be easy to assume the seven Principles are a flat list, each carrying the same weight, to be balanced against each other case by case. That assumption is wrong, and the SRA is explicit about it: where two or more Principles come into conflict, those which safeguard the wider public interest — in the rule of law and the administration of justice, and in public trust in the profession — take precedence over those concerned with an individual client.

The logic is straightforward once stated. A solicitor's duty to any one client exists only because the profession as a whole is trusted to operate within, and to uphold, the legal system. If 'acting in the client's best interests' could be stretched to justify undermining the rule of law, the exception would swallow the rule that makes the profession trustworthy in the first place.

This is why Principle 7 — the one most students instinctively reach for — cannot be used to justify a breach of Principle 1. A solicitor cannot claim to be acting in a client's best interests by helping that client deceive a court, obstruct justice, or otherwise undermine the legal system the client is relying on.

components.definition: Where SRA Principles conflict, the Principles safeguarding the rule of law, the administration of justice, and public trust in the profession take precedence over Principles concerned with the individual client — most importantly, Principle 7 cannot override Principle 1 or Principle 2.

interaction.prompt: Put these Principles in order from 'most protective of the wider public interest' to 'most focused on the individual client', reflecting how the SRA resolves a conflict between them.
items: Rule of law and administration of justice (Principle 1)
Public trust and confidence in the profession (Principle 2)
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the hierarchy. Principle 1 sits at the top because everything else — including the client relationship itself — depends on the legal system functioning properly.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Re-order with the justice-facing Principles first: the rule of law and administration of justice (1), then public trust (2), then the personal-quality Principles (3–5), with the client-facing Principle 7 last. That order is what decides a conflict.

parts.heading: Where the trap sits: Principle 7 is not a trump card
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through a realistic dilemma before naming the rule
body: Imagine a client asks their solicitor to backdate a contract so it appears to have been signed before a regulatory deadline that has now passed. The client is insistent: this is what's in their best interests, and Principle 7 requires the solicitor to act in the best interests of each client.

Students who haven't internalised the hierarchy sometimes reason from Principle 7 outward — 'the client wants this, so doing it serves their interests, so it's required'. That reasoning stops at the wrong Principle. Backdating a document to mislead a regulator or a court is a direct assault on the proper administration of justice: Principle 1. The solicitor who does what the client asks has not correctly applied Principle 7 at all — they have simply let it override a Principle that cannot be overridden.

The correct analysis is to identify every Principle engaged by the facts, then ask whether any of them are in tension. Only once you've spotted the tension does the hierarchy do its work: here, Principle 1 wins outright, and the solicitor must refuse — however strongly the client insists it serves their interests.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often conclude that because Principle 7 requires acting in the client's best interests, a solicitor should generally do what the client wants unless it is clearly unlawful.
components.whyItsWrong: Principle 7 never operates in isolation. It is always read subject to the Principles that protect the rule of law, the administration of justice, and public trust — a client's wishes, however sincerely held, cannot convert a breach of those Principles into something Principle 7 requires or excuses.

interaction.prompt: A client asks their solicitor to withhold a document from disclosure that damages the client's case but which the client is legally obliged to disclose. What does the Principles hierarchy require?
options: The solicitor must comply, because Principle 7 requires acting in the client's best interests
The solicitor must refuse, because complying would breach Principle 1 and Principle 7 cannot override it
The solicitor may comply if the client confirms the instruction in writing
The solicitor should ask the court for permission before deciding
interaction.trapExplanation: The instinct to reach for Principle 7 first is exactly the trap this lesson exists to break. Written confirmation of an instruction does not change its legal character — concealing a document that must be disclosed undermines the administration of justice regardless of how clearly the client asked for it.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Principle 1 protects the administration of justice and cannot be displaced by a client instruction, however clearly given.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at which Principle is actually in tension here. Concealing a disclosable document engages Principle 1 (administration of justice) directly — and Principle 1 outranks Principle 7.

parts.heading: Public trust: the Principle that reaches beyond the file
parts.voice: direct — sets up scope before the final application part
body: Principle 2 — upholding public trust and confidence in the profession — is unusual among the seven because it isn't confined to how a solicitor treats their own clients or conducts their own matters. It protects something collective: the public's willingness to trust solicitors generally.

This gives Principle 2 a wider reach than students expect. Conduct that damages public confidence in the profession can, in principle, engage this Principle even where no specific client has been harmed and no specific rule of professional conduct on a file has been broken — because the harm is to trust in the profession as an institution, not to any one transaction.

Keep this in mind as a category, even though the detailed limits of how far 'public trust' extends into a solicitor's life outside work are explored properly in the lesson on the Code of Conduct's duties to the court and the regulator. For now, the exam-relevant point is simpler: Principle 2 sits alongside Principle 1 at the top of the hierarchy, and both outrank the client-facing Principles when they conflict.

components.definition: Principle 2 protects the standing of the solicitors' profession as a whole in the eyes of the public, not merely the solicitor's own client relationships — and, together with Principle 1, ranks above the client-facing Principles in any conflict.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Principle 2 (public trust) can, in principle, be engaged even when the solicitor's own client has suffered no harm at all?
sliderLabels: No — harm to a specific client is always required
Yes — Principle 2 protects trust in the profession generally
interaction.explanation: Principle 2 is drafted around confidence in the profession and in legal services generally, not around the treatment of a specific client — that is what distinguishes it from Principle 7.

parts.heading: Applying the hierarchy under exam pressure
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the dilemma, then works through the reasoning
body: SQE1 fact patterns rarely announce 'this is a Principle 1 versus Principle 7 conflict' in so many words. You're expected to spot the tension yourself, in a paragraph of plausible client instructions, and reason to the correct outcome under time pressure.

A reliable method: first, identify every Principle arguably engaged by the facts. Second, ask whether any of them point in different directions. Third, if they do, apply the hierarchy — the justice-facing and trust-facing Principles (1 and 2) outrank the personal-quality Principles (3–5), which in turn are not simply overridden by Principle 7 either; Principle 7 operates only within the space the other Principles leave open.

Practise this method now, because the next two lessons — on the detailed Code of Conduct — build directly on it. Almost every conduct scenario in this module reduces, at bottom, to identifying which Principle is really at stake and whether a client's wishes can lawfully satisfy it.

components.title: Resolving a Principles conflict
components.description: The reasoning sequence for a fact pattern where Principles appear to conflict.

nodes.label: Identify every Principle arguably engaged by the facts
Do any of them point in different directions?
No → apply the engaged Principle(s) directly
Yes → is Principle 1 or 2 (justice/public trust) among them?
Yes → Principle 1/2 prevails over the client-facing Principle
No → weigh the remaining Principles (3–6) against Principle 7 on the specific facts

components.textAlternative: First identify every Principle arguably engaged by the facts. If none conflict, apply the engaged Principle directly. If they conflict, check whether Principle 1 or 2 is among them — if so, that Principle prevails over the client-facing Principle 7. If neither Principle 1 nor 2 is engaged, weigh the remaining Principles against Principle 7 on the specific facts.

interaction.prompt: A client instructs their solicitor to send a letter to an unrepresented opponent that the solicitor knows contains a misleading statement of the legal position, calculated to pressure the opponent into settling. Applying the Principles hierarchy, what should the solicitor do?
options: Send the letter, since acting in the client's best interests (Principle 7) is the solicitor's paramount duty
Refuse to send the letter as drafted, since knowingly misleading a third party engages Principle 1 and Principle 2, which outrank Principle 7
Send the letter but add a disclaimer that the client, not the solicitor, is responsible for its contents
Ask the client to sign a waiver before sending the letter
interaction.explanation: Knowingly misleading anyone — including an unrepresented opponent — engages both the proper administration of justice (Principle 1) and public trust in the profession (Principle 2). Neither a disclaimer nor a client waiver can convert this into something Principle 7 permits, because Principle 7 never authorises a breach of the higher-ranked Principles.

testPool.prompt: A trainee is asked to identify the SRA Principle that requires a solicitor to 'act with independence'. Which is it?
options: Principle 2
Principle 3
Principle 4
Principle 6
testPool.explanation: Independence is Principle 3, immediately after the two outward-facing Principles (rule of law, public trust) and before honesty and integrity.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best describes the legal status of the SRA Principles?
options: They are the fundamental ethical obligations set out in the SRA Standards and Regulations 2019, applying to every person the SRA regulates
They are non-binding guidance solicitors are encouraged, but not required, to follow
They are terms implied into every retainer between solicitor and client by statute
They apply only to solicitors in private practice, not those working in-house
testPool.explanation: The Principles are the mandatory foundation of the SRA Standards and Regulations 2019 and bind every person and firm the SRA regulates, including in-house solicitors, not merely those in private practice.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor's client insists that acting in his best interests (Principle 7) requires the solicitor to conceal a material fact from the court. Which of the following best states how the SRA resolves this?
options: Principle 7 prevails, because a solicitor's paramount duty is always to the client who instructs them
Principle 1 prevails, because Principles protecting the rule of law and administration of justice outrank client-facing Principles
Neither Principle applies until the court itself raises the issue
The solicitor should follow whichever Principle the client's written instructions specify
testPool.trapExplanation: Treating Principle 7 as an automatic 'paramount duty' is the single most common error in this area — Principle 7 is always subject to Principle 1 and Principle 2, not the other way round, and a client cannot instruct their way around that by putting it in writing.
testPool.explanation: Concealing a material fact from the court is a direct threat to the proper administration of justice, engaging Principle 1, which outranks Principle 7 whenever the two conflict.

testPool.prompt: A client tells her solicitor she intends to give false evidence at trial and asks the solicitor to help prepare her witness statement accordingly. What should the solicitor do next?
options: Prepare the statement as instructed, since the client's version of events is a matter for the court, not the solicitor, to assess
Decline to prepare a statement containing evidence the solicitor knows to be false, and advise the client of the consequences of giving false evidence
Prepare the statement but flag internally that it may be inaccurate
Ask a colleague to prepare the statement instead, so the solicitor is not personally responsible
testPool.explanation: Knowingly helping a client put false evidence before a court breaches Principle 1 (administration of justice) and cannot be justified by reference to Principle 7. Passing the task to a colleague does not remove the underlying problem, since the firm would still be facilitating false evidence.

testPool.prompt: Principle 4 requires a solicitor to 'act with honesty', while Principle 5 requires acting 'with integrity'. Which of the following best captures the distinction the SRA draws between the two?
options: Honesty and integrity mean exactly the same thing and are listed separately only for emphasis
Honesty is about not being deceptive or misleading, whereas integrity is the wider requirement to adhere to proper professional and ethical standards, even where no dishonesty is involved
Integrity only applies to solicitors holding a supervisory role within a firm
Honesty applies to dealings with clients only, while integrity applies to dealings with the court only
testPool.explanation: Honesty is a subjective, factual concept concerned with truthfulness; integrity is broader and objective, capturing adherence to ethical standards more generally — a solicitor can act dishonestly without lacking integrity in some other respect, and vice versa, which is why the SRA lists them as separate Principles.

testPool.prompt: How many Principles are set out in the SRA Standards and Regulations 2019?
options: Five
Six
Seven
Nine
testPool.explanation: There are seven Principles, numbered 1 to 7, and SQE1 questions frequently expect you to identify the correct number when a Principle is described.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor discovers, partway through a hearing, that a document already before the court contains a figure the client knows to be wrong. The client asks the solicitor to say nothing, because correcting it would damage the client's case. What is the solicitor's best course of action?
options: Say nothing, since the client's instructions under Principle 7 must be followed once litigation has begun
Take steps to correct the position with the court, since allowing it to stand uncorrected engages Principle 1 and cannot be excused by Principle 7
Wait until after judgment to raise the issue, to avoid prejudicing the client mid-hearing
Correct it only if opposing counsel raises the discrepancy first
testPool.trapExplanation: The idea that a duty of confidentiality or client loyalty under Principle 7 'locks in' once proceedings start is a common misreading — no stage of litigation converts a breach of Principle 1 into something the client's wishes can authorise.
testPool.explanation: Allowing a court to proceed on a figure the solicitor knows to be wrong, at the client's request, is a breach of Principle 1 regardless of the procedural stage reached, and delay does not cure it.

testPool.prompt: A firm's recruitment process consistently screens out otherwise well-qualified candidates from a particular background, with no objective justification, because a partner believes they 'won't fit the culture'. Which Principle is most clearly engaged?
options: Principle 3 (independence)
Principle 4 (honesty)
Principle 6 (equality, diversity and inclusion)
Principle 7 (best interests of each client)
testPool.explanation: Principle 6 requires a solicitor and firm to act in a way that encourages equality, diversity and inclusion; an unjustified recruitment practice that screens out candidates by background is a direct engagement of that Principle, independent of any client relationship.

testPool.prompt: Principle 3 requires a solicitor to 'act with independence'. Which of the following scenarios best illustrates a breach of this Principle?
options: A solicitor declines to take on a new client due to a lack of capacity
A solicitor allows a powerful, high-fee-paying client to dictate legal advice that the solicitor's own professional judgement does not support
A solicitor charges a client the fee agreed in the retainer letter
A solicitor refers a client to a more experienced colleague for a specialist matter
testPool.explanation: Independence means the solicitor's professional judgement must not be subordinated to outside pressure, including pressure from a valuable client — allowing fee income or client influence to dictate advice contrary to the solicitor's own judgement breaches Principle 3.

testPool.prompt: 'Act in the best interests of each client' is which numbered SRA Principle?
options: Principle 4
Principle 5
Principle 6
Principle 7
testPool.explanation: This is Principle 7, listed last of the seven — a position that reflects its subordination to the profession-facing and public-facing Principles that precede it.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best describes the reach of Principle 2 (public trust and confidence)?
options: It applies only to conduct on a client's file, and never to conduct that has no specific client attached to it
It protects public confidence in the profession as a whole, and can in principle be engaged even where no individual client has been harmed
It applies only to partners and senior solicitors, not to trainees or junior fee earners
It is fully superseded by Principle 7 once a retainer is in place
testPool.trapExplanation: Treating Principle 2 as confined to specific client files understates it — the Principle protects trust in the profession as an institution, which is exactly why it, together with Principle 1, outranks the purely client-facing Principle 7.
testPool.explanation: Principle 2 protects public trust and confidence in the profession generally, not merely in the outcome of any one client relationship, and it applies to every regulated person regardless of seniority.

testPool.prompt: A client asks their solicitor to make a without-notice application to the court but to deliberately omit a fact that the client knows would weigh against granting the order, on the basis that omitting it serves the client's interests. What is the solicitor's best course of action?
options: Comply, since without-notice applications are decided on whatever material the applicant chooses to present
Refuse to omit the material fact, since a without-notice application carries a duty of full and frank disclosure that engages Principle 1
Comply, provided the omission is not the deciding factor in the judge's decision
Ask the client to confirm the instruction in writing before proceeding
testPool.explanation: A without-notice application carries a well-recognised duty of full and frank disclosure precisely because the other side is absent; deliberately withholding an adverse fact undermines the proper administration of justice and engages Principle 1, which Principle 7 cannot override.

testPool.prompt: A firm argues that because no individual Principle has been breached on the facts of a matter, there can be no disciplinary issue at all. Which of the following best evaluates that argument?
options: The argument is correct — the Principles are the only source of professional obligations a solicitor owes
The argument is incomplete — the Principles sit alongside more detailed rules in the SRA Code of Conduct, which can be engaged even where no single Principle is obviously breached in isolation
The argument is correct provided the client has not complained
The argument is incorrect only where the matter involves litigation
testPool.explanation: The Principles are the foundation of the regulatory framework but are supplemented by the more granular obligations in the SRA Code of Conduct, which give practical effect to the Principles in specific situations — a matter can raise a Code issue even where the Principles alone seem satisfied on a broad reading.

testPool.prompt: A client asks their solicitor to draft a letter before action that overstates the strength of the client's claim in order to intimidate the recipient into an early settlement, but which stops short of any statement the solicitor knows to be factually false. Is this most likely to be regulated by the Principles hierarchy discussed in this lesson?
options: Yes — robust or persuasive advocacy for a client's position is not, without more, a breach of Principle 1 or Principle 2, so this falls within the scope Principle 7 leaves open
No — any letter drafted with the aim of pressuring a recipient automatically breaches Principle 1
Yes — but only because the letter is addressed to a represented party
No — Principle 6 is engaged whenever a letter is one-sided
testPool.explanation: The hierarchy only bites where Principles genuinely conflict. Firm, persuasive advocacy that does not cross into dishonesty or misleading statements of fact does not, without more, engage Principle 1 or Principle 2 — so acting robustly in the client's interests under Principle 7 remains permissible here, unlike the misleading-letter scenario in the lecture.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating Principle 7 (best interests of each client) as if it were the solicitor's paramount duty. It isn't — it operates only within the space left open once Principles 1 and 2 are satisfied, and no client instruction, however clear or however firmly put in writing, can convert a breach of the rule of law or public trust into something the client's best interests require.
